title: Olympiad Day 7: Two Nodirbeks, one golden mission
summary: Uzbekistan keeps marching towards gold as its two Nodirbeks continue to deliver With the finish line beginning to come into view, every half-point is becoming increasingly valuable in Samarkand. Uzbekistan continue to lead the Open section, with the two Nodirbeks playing a central role in the hosts’ impressive run, while a crowded chasing pack is still fighting to stay within striking distance. With only a handful of rounds remaining, the pressure is rising and there is little room for a slip. In the Women’s section, China and Kazakhstan remain locked in a tie at the top after their direct encounter, while India, Georgia, Armenia and several other strong teams continue to battle for position. Surprises are becoming increasingly costly at this stage of the Olympiad, as every match can have a major impact on the medal race. Let’s take a closer look at the action from the playing hall. Ceremonial moves across the playing hall Ceremonial opening moves are generally performed on the top boards, but occasionally politicians and dignitaries from other countries travel to the Olympiad and, naturally, would like to open the game for their own teams. That, however, involves a little extra coordination. The media has to move swiftly from board to board, which is no easy task in a 163-meter-long playing hall! The first dignitary to make a ceremonial move was Mrs. Veronique Herminie, First Lady of the Republic of Seychelles, who opened her country’s women’s team game on board two with 1.e4. Media attention then shifted to the match between Barbados and Aruba, where Mr. Chad Blackman, Minister of Educational Transformation and Member of Parliament for St. James North, Barbados, made the ceremonial move on board one. The third ceremonial move took place on board one of the Costa Rica–Latvia match. Mr. Donald Rojas Fernández, National Director of the Costa Rican Institute of Sport and Recreation, opened the game for Costa Rica’s number-one player, IM Leonardo Valdés Romero. Finally, everyone hurried back to the top board, where Mr. Husen Tuxtaev, Deputy Governor of the Samarkand Region for Youth Policy, Social Development, and Spiritual and Educational Affairs, opened Nodirbek Abdusattorov’s game with 1.e3, amidst a flurry of photographers and television cameras. “A very solid move,” remarked Christian Chirila from the commentary booth. Peter Svidler immediately added his own humorous assessment: “Everything is protected – 1.e4 puts a pawn on an unprotected square. That is just not on!” Open section Uzbekistan take another step towards gold It is always interesting to see how players react after a much-needed free day. Some take the opportunity to play sports, others explore Samarkand, and some even join an online “Titled Tuesday”. Most, however, simply use the break to catch up on some well-deserved rest and recharge their batteries for the latter stages of the tournament. Yet a brisk walk around the venue quickly made it apparent that many players are still feeling the strain, particularly those who have had little opportunity to take a round off. Uzbekistan, however, appear to be the exception. All five members of their squad are young and energetic, and they have shown an impressive ability to bring their A-game to the board day after day. This afternoon, they took another giant step towards gold by defeating China 3–1 in convincing fashion. Uzbekistan won with White on boards one and three, while the other two games were drawn, giving the hosts another emphatic team victory against one of the strongest contenders in the field. Abdusattorov strikes, Yakubboev keeps rolling On board one, Nodirbek Abdusattorov, now on an impressive 5.5/7, handed Ding Liren his first defeat of the tournament. His victory was built on excellent opening preparation, which gave him a huge advantage on the clock and allowed him to play with considerable time in hand throughout the game. Although it was not easy to catch him immediately after such an intense battle, FIDE’s own Charlize van Zyl was the first reporter to get hold of Abdusattorov for a quick interview once he had managed to catch his breath. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eHkR1oSOMkw Meanwhile, the second Nodirbek in the Uzbekistan team, Yakubboev, ground down Yu Yangyi in a tricky endgame to score his fifth win in his last six games. At this rate, it would hardly be surprising to see him fighting for an individual medal as well. Armenia hold USA as India keep their hopes alive Combined with Armenia’s result, the victory leaves Uzbekistan two full match points clear of their nearest challengers, while they also enjoy a substantial advantage on the tiebreak. With four rounds still to play, the hosts have put themselves in an extremely strong position in the race for gold In fact, even though they could not quite keep pace with Uzbekistan, Armenia’s 2–2 draw against the United States was a massive result for the underdogs. Awonder Liang finally picked up his second win on board four, while Wesley So seriously misplayed a tricky rook ending involving passed pawns and was forced to resign against Robert Hovhannisyan. Although their average rating is significantly lower than that of the top seeds, Armenia are an extremely tight-knit team who know each other very well and have collected numerous medals in major team events. They may not always attract the same attention as the top seeds, but they can never be taken lightly. After their defeat to Uzbekistan, India had little choice but to beat England if they were to keep their medal hopes alive. They duly delivered a 2.5–1.5 victory, winning on boards one and four. Gukesh D, in particular, continued his outstanding tournament, moving to an impressive 6/7 and firmly putting himself in the conversation for an individual medal. England, meanwhile, opted to rest third-board Gawain Jones – although he was still very much involved in the match, taking his place as captain! title: Commonwealth Chess Association partners with Chessveda to expand digital chess across Commonwealth nations
summary: Samarkand, Uzbekistan, September 23, 2026: The Commonwealth Chess Association (CCA) has entered into a partnership with Chessveda, an integrated digital chess platform, to promote and expand chess activities across Commonwealth nations. The partnership agreement was signed on the sidelines of the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand by Mr. Bharat Singh Chauhan, Chairman of the Commonwealth Chess Association, and Adv. Nandan Jha, Chairman of Chessveda. The signing ceremony was attended by presidents of chess federations from Commonwealth countries, along with Grandmasters, International Masters and other members of the international chess community. The partnership will enable the Commonwealth Chess Association and Chessveda to collaborate in organising online chess tournaments, Chess Olympiads and other chess-related events, creating additional opportunities for players, coaches, organisers and chess communities across Commonwealth nations. The collaboration is also aimed at strengthening the digital dimension of chess and providing players from different countries with greater opportunities to participate in competitive chess irrespective of geographical boundaries. Speaking on the occasion, Commonwealth Chess Association Chairman Bharat Singh Chauhan said, “We are delighted to formalise this partnership with Chessveda and welcome them as an official partner for online chess. Digital platforms are opening new avenues for participation in chess, and this collaboration will enable us to provide more opportunities for players and chess communities across Commonwealth nations to participate and compete.” “The Commonwealth Chess Association is committed to promoting chess among all its member federations and to creating wider opportunities for players of different ages and levels. Our association with Chessveda will help us explore new formats and initiatives while complementing our existing over the board chess activities,” he added. Chessveda Chairman Adv. Nandan Jha said, “We envision organising online Chess Olympiads and other major championships at a global level. Our aim is to bring the global potential of chess and online chess to a wider audience while providing grassroots talent with opportunities to compete on global platforms and stages. Through this initiative, we hope to help players showcase their talent internationally and contribute to taking chess to greater heights.” Chessveda’s digital platform brings together online chess playing, learning and training, tournaments and competitions, coaching, chess communities, news and other chess-related content. The platform seeks to provide an integrated digital environment where players can learn, play, compete, connect and develop. For the Commonwealth Chess Association, the partnership represents an important step towards expanding its digital outreach and developing new avenues for chess participation across its member nations. The collaboration is expected to support the organisation of online and hybrid chess initiatives and provide additional platforms for players to engage in competitive chess. The CCA will work with Chessveda to explore and develop suitable tournaments, championships and other chess activities that can benefit players and chess communities across the Commonwealth. The partnership comes at a significant moment for Commonwealth chess, with the 46th Chess Olympiad bringing together players, officials and chess administrators from across the world in Samarkand. Through the collaboration, the Commonwealth Chess Association and Chessveda aim to create new opportunities for participation, competition and engagement, while contributing to the continued development and wider reach of chess across Commonwealth nations.

title: Beyond the Board: FIDE Women’s Chess Commission maps pathways, progress and the future of women’s chess
summary: The FIDE Commission for Women’s Chess (WOM) held its 2026 Commission Meeting on September 22 in Samarkand, bringing together FIDE leadership, Commission members, invited speakers and guests to discuss the development and future of women’s chess. Themed “Beyond the Board: Women, Innovation and the Business of Chess,” the meeting explored opportunities for women across the wider chess ecosystem – from playing and education to media, entrepreneurship, leadership and business – while reviewing the Commission’s projects and recognizing the people contributing to its work. Women in chess: Beyond playing Opening the meeting, Dana Reizniece, Acting Chair of the FIDE Management Board, reflected on the progress made in recent years and stressed that increasing women’s representation in chess means looking far beyond the number of female players. “When we speak about women in chess, it’s not only about players. It is about so many other professions that we see in the chess world where women are underrepresented: as an arbiter, a trainer, a fair play officer, a commentator, and in the leadership positions. And this is our common task to change.” Reizniece highlighted the work undertaken through initiatives for girls, training programmes, projects supporting refugees and efforts to create new women’s Olympiad teams. She also pointed to the record number of women’s teams participating in Samarkand as an encouraging sign of progress. The meeting then featured a special session with the three candidates for the FIDE presidency: Wadim Rosenstein, Timur Turlov and Jan Henric Buettner. With women’s chess forming an important part of FIDE’s activities and the wider chess community, the presence of all three candidates gave the meeting a chance to address the subject within the broader conversation about the federation’s future. Building a safe environment for women and girls GM Viswanathan Anand, FIDE Interim President, reflected on the work of the Women’s Commission over the past four years and the continued growth in female participation. Anand also gave the discussion a personal dimension when speaking about the ChessMom initiative, recalling that he himself had learned chess from his mother. He stressed that alongside increasing participation, creating an environment in which women and girls feel safe must remain a long-term priority. “We are very committed to making chess a very safe space. It has to be a place where, especially for a parent of a young girl, you don’t have to think about it – it’s completely okay to send my daughter to play chess. That’s the long-term goal.” Anand also highlighted initiatives including the online women’s chess festival and Women’s Chess Day, and emphasized the importance of continuing to raise both participation and the profile of women in chess. Tris-Ann Richards: Safeguarding must be a priority Tris-Ann Richards, Chair of the FIDE Commission for Women’s Chess, then presented an overview of the Commission’s work and projects over recent years, while also turning attention to one of the most serious issues discussed during the meeting: safeguarding. Richards referred to research conducted through the Commission, including the recently completed global survey. According to the figures she presented, two in five of women surveyed reported having faced sexual harassment within a chess setting, three-quarters reported experiencing discrimination or harassment, and almost half had considered leaving chess. For Richards, the findings reinforce the need for safeguarding procedures to become an integral part of the way chess events and organizations operate. “I’m very adamant on a clear policy being established to deal with such incidents, a clear FIDE policy, and that each national federation has procedures to deal with incidents like this when they occur. What I hope and will work towards is that every event, every major chess tournament, will make public what their safeguard measures are.” Richards also advocated safeguarding training for officials, including arbiters and trainers, independent investigative procedures, and clearer information at tournaments on how participants can report harassment or discrimination. At the same time, she pointed to progress in women’s participation and acknowledged the work of Commission members and supporters, while stressing that further work remains. From chess player to chess professional The programme continued with reports and presentations demonstrating the different ways women can participate in and build careers through chess. Ulkar Umudova presented the Queens & Princesses initiative and its latest developments, highlighting a project designed to create opportunities for women and girls to participate, compete and connect through chess. WIM Fiona Steil-Antoni then spoke on “From Chess Player to Chess Entrepreneur: Building Opportunities On and Off the Board.” A chess player herself, Steil-Antoni has also developed a professional career in the game as a commentator, interviewer and host, offering an example of how a connection to chess can evolve into professional opportunities beyond tournament play. The focus then moved to motherhood and chess. Francisco Cruz, Deputy President of the Confederation of Chess for Americas and a WOM Commission member, presented the ChessMom initiative, which addresses some of the challenges faced by chess-playing mothers and explores how the chess community can better support them. The business of chess Another dimension of the “Beyond the Board” theme came from Sagar Shah, whose presentation, “The Business of Chess: Opportunities, Investment & The Future of the Chess Industry,” examined the expanding professional ecosystem around the game. With chess increasingly creating opportunities in media, technology, education, events, content creation and entrepreneurship, the presentation looked at where the chess industry is heading and what new professional possibilities its development can create. The Commission reports continued with Susana Alexandra Gonçalves, Marco Biagioli and Monalisha Khamboo (pictured below), who presented updates on WOM projects and ongoing work. title: Total Chess World Championship Tour announces six more stars for Budapest pilot
summary: Hungary, Budapest, September 23, 2026 – Total Chess World Championship Tour, the FIDE-approved global event conceptualised by Norway Chess, has announced six more leading international chess players who will compete in the official pilot event in Budapest from November 10 to 20, 2026. The field of 24 players for the Pilot event is now complete.  The latest additions to the field are Levon Aronian, Liem Le, Jorden van Foreest, Abhimanyu Mishra, Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and Andrew Hong, further strengthening an elite line-up featuring some of the biggest names in world chess. They join a field led by World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen, alongside World No. 3 Fabiano Caruana and a host of leading players from across the global chess community. Hosted at the iconic Anantara New York Palace Budapest Hotel, the pilot will showcase the unique Total Chess format, bringing together Fast Classic, Rapid and Blitz in a single championship. The event serves as the official pilot ahead of the inaugural global Total Chess World Championship Tour season in 2027. Expressing his eagerness to compete in this format, Levon Aronian said: “As one of the more experienced players in chess, I’m excited to be part of this new and innovative format. Bringing Fast Classic, Rapid and Blitz together creates a very different challenge for players. I’m looking forward to seeing how the Total Chess World Championship Tour develops and what it can bring to the future of elite chess.” Kjell Madland, CEO of Total Chess World Championship Tour, said: “The addition of these six exceptional players makes an already outstanding field even stronger. Their experience, personalities and different approaches to the game reflect exactly what Total Chess is about. It brings the very best of chess together across formats and creates a championship that can engage a new generation of fans. Budapest is an important first step as we build towards the global tour in 2027.” The Total Chess World Championship Tour is designed to determine the FIDE World Combined Champion, bringing together performance across the three principal formats of elite chess – Fast Classic, Rapid and Blitz.  The Budapest pilot will provide the first competitive showcase of the concept before the Tour launches its inaugural global season in 2027, with elite events planned across leading international cities. The Budapest field brings together 24 elite players, representing a diverse mix of established world champions, leading contenders, rising stars and some of the most exciting young talent in the game. Players confirmed (ranked by their September 2026 FIDE standard rating) Magnus Carlsen (Norway) – World No. 1 Fabiano Caruana (United States) – World No. 3 Wesley So (United States) – World No. 5 Vincent Keymer (Germany) – World No. 6 Nodirbek Abdusattorov (Uzbekistan) – World No. 7 R Praggnanandhaa (India) – World No. 8 Arjun Erigaisi (India) – World No. 9 Anish Giri (Netherlands) – World No. 10 Alireza Firouzja (France) – World No. 11 Jan-Krzysztof Duda (Poland) – World No. 13 Liem Le (Vietnam) – World No. 18 Richard Rapport (Hungary) – World No. 19 Levon Aronian (USA) – World No. 20 Hans Moke Niemann (United States) – World No. 21 Shakhriyar Mamedyarov (Azerbaijan) – World No. 22 Ian Nepomniachtchi (FIDE) – World No. 23 Maxime Vachier-Lagrave (France) – World No. 24 Jorden van Foreest (Netherlands) – World No. 30 Haik M. Martirosyan (Armenia) – World No. 50 Vladislav Artemiev (FIDE) – World No. 65 Abhimanyu Mishra (USA) – World No. 96 – World’s Youngest Grandmaster Andrew Hong (USA) – World No. 152 Bibisara Assaubayeva (Kazakhstan) – Women’s World No. 5 Vaishali Rameshbabu (India) – Women’s World No. 16 About the format The Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot introduces a groundbreaking competition format designed to identify the world’s most complete chess player by combining Fast Classic, Rapid and Blitz into a single championship. The pilot event will bring together 24 elite players, who will begin the tournament in a group stage comprising four groups of six players each. Every group follows a double round-robin format over five days, with players contesting ten Fast Classic games (45 minutes plus a 30-second increment). Victories earn three points, while draws are worth one point. A nine-round Blitz Swiss tournament held before the competition determines tie-break rankings. Following the group stage, players progress into knockout brackets based on their finishing positions. Each knockout match is played over two days and tests competitors across all three disciplines – four Blitz games (3+2), two Rapid games (15+10) and one Fast Classic game (45+30) – with weighted scoring rewarding success in longer formats. The four highest-ranked players across the Tour qualify for the Grand Final, where semifinals and the championship match determine the inaugural FIDE World Combined Champion. Should a knockout match remain tied, an Armageddon game is used to decide the winner, ensuring every contest produces a definitive result. The format rewards consistency, versatility and excellence across every major discipline of elite chess. Three disciplines. One champion. One global tour. The journey begins in Budapest. For more information, visit: https://www.totalchess.com/ About Total Chess Total Chess is a global championship platform established to redefine elite competitive chess for the modern era. Developed by Norway Chess and approved by FIDE, the Total Chess World Championship Tour introduces a unified format that crowns the world’s ultimate champion by testing excellence across three disciplines: Fast Classic, Rapid and Blitz. The Tour will bring together the world’s top 24 men and women players to compete across four premier international events hosted in leading global cities. Designed to elevate the sport’s commercial appeal and fan engagement, Total Chess combines world-class competition with innovation, technology and immersive spectator experiences to create a new benchmark for professional chess. With a vision to make chess one of the world’s most engaging and commercially sustainable sports, Total Chess aims to expand the game’s global footprint, inspire the next generation of players, and connect millions of fans through a dynamic championship that celebrates intelligence, strategy and sporting excellence. For more information or press inquiries, contact press@totalchess.com.
